title: Hallucination governance: Sanctions target inquiry failures
desc: Maintains human accountability and broad verification while courts dispute AI-specific disclosure and restrictions.

kps.k: Human accountability remains the governing principle for legal AI use.
kps.d: The cluster treats AI as an assistive tool, not a substitute for professional or judicial responsibility. Existing duties of competence, candor, confidentiality, supervision and reasonable inquiry continue to bind the lawyer who signs or relies on work, even when another lawyer, a nonlawyer or an AI system produced it. Judges likewise retain adjudicative authority, and self-represented litigants remain accountable for their filings. Verification requires independent judgment: users must consult authoritative sources, read cited authorities, confirm their validity and determine whether they support the asserted propositions.

qs.q: Second, a lawyer must exercise                  independent professional judgment by reviewing, verifying, and                  correcting AI-generated outputs consistent with the learning and skill                  reasonably necessary for the representation.
qs.a: Practical Guidance for the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in the Practice of Law · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: The California Court of Appeal put it well: “To state the obvious, it is a fundamental duty of attorneys to read the legal authorities they cite in appellate briefs or any other court filings to determine that the authorities stand for the propositions for which they are cited.” Noland, 114 Cal.
qs.a: Lnu v. Blanche, No. 24-4790 (9th Cir. June 3, 2026) · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Hallucination cases establish concrete risks but do not measure general model reliability.
kps.d: Reported proceedings document nonexistent authorities, invented quotations, false facts and real decisions misrepresented as supporting propositions they do not establish. Misstatements attached to genuine cases may be harder to detect than fictitious citations. These incidents show harm from failed verification across lawyers, supervisors, experts, judges and self-represented litigants, but incident databases count identified court events rather than model error rates. Benchmark findings provide separate, tool- and task-specific evidence; they do not establish a universal hallucination rate, particularly for bespoke or inaccessible internal systems.

qs.q: This problem now often manifests as false quotes or statements of law attributed to real cases, rather than the more easily recognizable fake cases.
qs.a: Fletcher v. Experian Information Solutions, Inc. — Fifth Circuit AI-Sanctions Opinion · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: In one study, we documented that hallucinations with legal AI providers range from 17% to 33% in a benchmark dataset of realistic and challenging queries (e.g., bar exam and appellate litigation questions).
qs.a: ABA Task Force on Law and Artificial Intelligence — Year 1 Report on the Impact of AI on the Practice of Law (August 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: Technical safeguards can reduce some errors, but verification remains broader than citation checking.
kps.d: Retrieval augmentation, fine-tuning and curated legal databases may reduce fabricated sources, and experimental evidence indicates that retrieval-grounded tools can perform better on that failure mode. Other evidence finds that citation hallucinations have not consistently declined across model generations. Even perfect source matching would not establish that analysis is complete, unbiased, legally sound or appropriate to the facts and jurisdiction. The evidence therefore does not resolve how far technical progress will lower human review costs. Aggregate burdens could also rise if cheaper drafting increases the volume of filings and citations faster than per-output accuracy improves.

qs.q: Indeed, the randomized controlled trial discussed in Part I demonstrated that RAG-enabled AI tools could largely eliminate hallucinated sources in this way.
qs.a: Thinking Like a Lawyer in the Age of Generative AI: Cognitive Limits on AI Adoption Among Lawyers · Academia · 2025

qs.q: Through a controlled experiment querying eight generations of ChatGPT models on 92 legal drafting prompts, we find that hallucination rates are no longer consistently decreasing across model generations, with GPT-5.1 producing hallucinated citations at a significantly higher rate than the best mid-2024 GPT-4o release (p = 0.001).
qs.a: Who Checks the Citations? Benchmarking Legal Hallucination Detection · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Authorities disagree over whether ordinary rules need AI-specific disclosure or task restrictions.
kps.d: One position relies on technology-neutral professional duties, signature rules and existing sanctions powers, rejecting routine AI disclosure as redundant and increasingly difficult to define as AI becomes embedded in ordinary software. Another position adds notifications, human-review certifications, tool identification, recordkeeping, prior permission or targeted prohibitions to protect provenance and procedural integrity. Intermediate approaches trigger disclosure when AI functions like a co-author or when provenance is material. Some regimes impose stricter controls on witness evidence and expert reports than on routine research, drafting or administration. The central disagreement concerns which supplementary safeguards are warranted, not whether humans remain responsible.

qs.q: In doing so, we concluded that existing rules were sufficient to deter misconduct related to generative AI use, without the need for a rule specific to generative AI.
qs.a: Fletcher v. Experian Information Solutions, Inc. — Fifth Circuit AI-Sanctions Opinion · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: A Declaration is required when the role AI plays in the preparation of materials for the purpose of litigation resembles that of a co-author.
qs.a: Notice to the Parties and the Profession — The Use of Artificial Intelligence in Court Proceedings (amended) · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: Sanctions target deficient inquiry and conduct after discovery, not AI use by itself.
kps.d: Courts have imposed financial penalties, costs, discipline referrals, disqualification, suspension, struck filings and dismissal, but outcomes depend on the circumstances. Relevant factors include the seriousness and scale of false material, objective failure to investigate, bad faith, supervisory failures, disruption to proceedings and prior warnings. Responsibility can extend to signatories and supervisors who did not personally use the tool. Prompt admission, correction and cooperation may mitigate consequences; concealment, minimisation and continued reliance aggravate them. Some courts have declined immediate sanctions, particularly where the required mental state was absent, while warning that future misconduct may be penalised.

qs.q: Whether that conduct supports the imposition of various types of 14   sanctions requires a fact- and circumstance-specific analysis.
qs.a: Lacey v. State Farm General Ins. Co. — Special Master Order Sanctioning Ellis George and K&L Gates for AI-Generated Fake Citations · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: Candor after filing weighs heavily in mitigation; concealment or minimization aggravates the violation.
qs.a: Cassata v. Michael Macrina Architect, P.C. — AI sanctions decision, Suffolk County · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Effective governance requires organisational controls as well as individual care.
kps.d: The sources call for tool-specific competence, approved-use policies, training, assigned review responsibility, supervision, monitoring, audit trails where appropriate and periodic reassessment. A written policy alone does not establish compliance; courts may examine whether managing partners, heads of chambers and other supervisory lawyers implemented effective measures. Practical controls include checking primary sources, limiting autonomous actions, documenting correction procedures and clarifying responsibility across teams and collaborating firms.

qs.q: First, just as a lawyer must make reasonable efforts to ensure that a law firm has policies to reasonably assure that the conduct of a nonlawyer assistant is compatible with the lawyer’s own professional obligations, a lawyer must do the same for generative AI.
qs.a: Ethics Informational Packet — Technology: Florida Bar Ethics Opinions Related to Technology (including Opinion 24-1 on generative AI and Opinion 25-1) · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: Watson had consistently violated the AI policy since its inception.
qs.a: Billups v. Louisville Municipal School District — Sanctions Order (N.D. Miss.) · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Accuracy controls form only one part of a wider confidentiality and procedural-integrity framework.
kps.d: Verification does not prevent disclosure of client information, privilege risks, biased output, fabricated evidence or improper delegation of consequential decisions. Users must assess provider terms, retention and training practices, third-party access and security settings before entering protected information. Client consent may be appropriate when use of a third-party system would disclose confidential information, but not merely because AI is used without such disclosure. In judicial work, additional concerns include unrebutted extrajudicial information, automation bias, due process and the need to place human reasoning on the record. Emerging privilege treatment remains fact-specific and unsettled.

qs.q: No user may input into any generative AI program that does not operate on a private model —      by writing a prompt, uploading a document or file, or otherwise — any information that is      confidential, private, or privileged, or includes personally identifiable information or      protected health information, or is otherwise inappropriate for public release.
qs.a: Interim Policy on the Use of Artificial Intelligence (New York State Unified Court System) · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: The terms of service for any GenAI tool used should always be reviewed for confidentiality,     privacy, and security considerations.
qs.a: Addressing the Legal Challenges of AI: Year 2 Report on the Impact of AI on the Practice of Law · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Access-to-justice benefits remain plausible but collide with users’ limited capacity to verify.
kps.d: AI may provide low-cost explanations, procedural guidance and drafting assistance to people who otherwise lack legal help. Yet self-represented users often lack legal training, authoritative database access and the ability to decide whether a genuine authority supports a proposition. This creates tension between formal filing responsibility and practical verification capacity. Some approaches favour equal accuracy standards, certifications and sanctions to protect courts; others warn that strict mandates or bans could turn verification into an inaccessible condition of assistance and transfer checking costs to courts and opponents. Proposed responses include public legal data, automated citation checking, bounded user interfaces and targeted AI-literacy support, but the access gains remain largely prospective.

qs.q: Litigants rarely have the skills independently to verify legal information provided by AI chatbots and may not be aware that they are prone to error.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence (AI) — Guidance for Judicial Office Holders (refreshed 31 October 2025) · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: Third, automated verification tools could ease verification burdens of courts, with sufficient access to data, but also assist non-lawyers directly to verify citations in documents drafted with AI assistance.
qs.a: Who Checks the Citations? Benchmarking Legal Hallucination Detection · Academia · 2026

kps.k: The practical case is for bounded, task-sensitive adoption rather than blanket prohibition.
kps.d: Courts and professional guidance recognise potential uses in research, summarisation, document review, routine drafting, administration and accessibility, provided humans retain meaningful control. Experimental evidence suggests that benefits vary by task: tested tools improved speed on several assignments but produced no measurable speed or quality gain on one NDA-drafting task. Unchecked output also creates an asymmetry because plausible false material can be generated quickly while courts and opponents must research each citation and proposition. Organisations should therefore match tools to defined tasks, test consequential uses, preserve human review and treat efficiency claims as conditional rather than universal.

qs.q: The Undersigned does not aim to  suggest that AI is inherently bad or that its use by lawyers should be forbidden.
qs.a: Mid Central Operating Engineers Health & Welfare Fund v. HoosierVac LLC — Report & Recommendation ($15,000) and Order ($6,000) Sanctioning Counsel for AI-Fabricated Citations in Three Briefs · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: While one party can create a fake legal brief          at the click of a button, the opposing party and court must parse through the case          names, citations, and points of law to determine which parts, if any, are true.
qs.a: The Promise and the Peril of the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Litigation · Academia · 2025

vlens.an: The curated academia-and-research sources broadly accept the proposition’s core: legal AI remains human-in-the-loop; verification requires substantive professional judgment rather than citation matching alone; and sanctions generally respond to deficient inquiry, supervision, candor or correction rather than AI use by itself. Collectively, they materially develop that account through controlled experiments, incident analysis and normative proposals. Their main extensions concern task-specific performance, verification burdens that may grow with filing volume, organisational controls, legal education, potential erosion of lawyers’ reasoning skills, malpractice and insurance exposure, and the access-to-justice problem that self-represented litigants may be formally accountable yet structurally unable to verify legal output. Material variation concerns supplementary governance. Some favour technology-neutral duties and oppose routine disclosure, certifications or bans as redundant and difficult to define; others support certifications, automated checking, public legal-data access, literacy programmes and targeted restrictions, especially for evidence, expert reports or courts serving unrepresented parties. Some sources are more optimistic that technical improvements and sanctions will suffice, while others find persistent citation fabrication or argue that verification cannot ensure overall work quality. One scholarship-focused source redirects from accuracy toward whether machine-written work can evidence authorial understanding, and fragmentary excerpts from a few sources do not disclose a governance position. These differences concern the scope and institutional support for verification, not the general principle of continuing human responsibility. Because the corpus is curated, this synthesis characterises only the supplied sources and does not establish the prevalence of these views across academia or research.

qs.q: These limitations indicate that GenAI models should be treated as ‘human-in- the-loop’ technologies, where users are responsible for identifying hallucinations and verifying output accuracy.
qs.a: The Promise and the Peril of the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Litigation · Academia · 2025

vlens.an: These selected traditional-law-firm sources accept the cluster’s principal proposition that humans remain accountable for AI-assisted legal work and that verification and procedural integrity cannot be displaced by the technology. They also materially extend it in two directions. First, the SDNY report adds a concrete, fact-specific privilege risk involving client-created AI documents sent to counsel, supporting the cluster’s broader confidentiality framework while stressing that the ruling was from the bench, lacked a written opinion, and did not establish a categorical rule for all AI-generated material. Second, the 2024 trends source develops the procedural-integrity analysis through deepfake authentication risks and possible certification of client-supplied material. Internal variation concerns the form and likely duration of safeguards rather than the governing principle: one account highlights emerging AI-specific risks, while the other reports support for technology-neutral filing rules and predicts that greater model accuracy may reduce heightened AI-specific verification requirements. That prediction does not displace ordinary verification or sanctions for deficient conduct. Because this is a curated pair of sources, the assessment describes their shared orientation and differences without implying prevalence across law firms generally.

qs.q: District Court for the Southern District of New York ruled from the bench that documents a client created using a commercial generative AI tool and sent to his lawyer were not protected by privilege.
qs.a: SDNY Rules AI-Generated Documents Are Not Protected by Privilege · Law firms · 2026

qs.q: The court further cautioned that “I used AI” would not serve as an excuse for otherwise sanctionable conduct.
qs.a: GenAI Trends in the Legal Profession in 2024 · Law firms · 2024

vlens.an: This curated set of market-analysis, consultancy and press sources generally accepts the proposition’s core: AI-assisted legal work remains subject to human verification, professional supervision and accountability, while fabricated authorities create concrete litigation consequences. Common reasons include reported sanctions and overturned decisions, lawyers’ continuing responsibility for signed filings, and the practical burden that unchecked material transfers to courts and opposing parties. Collectively, the sources materially extend the proposition by tracing downstream malpractice-insurance exposure and by proposing controls for clients’ GenAI use, including documented warnings, confidentiality safeguards and transcription policies. There is meaningful internal variation: several press reports principally relay judicial positions rather than offer independent prescriptions; one source documents harms without taking a discernible position on sanctions or governance; some favour new guidelines or disclosure requirements without specifying their scope; and reporting on self-represented litigants balances court burdens against conditional access-to-justice benefits. The sources also show that consequences are not automatic: sanctions vary with verification failures, correction, cooperation and aggravating conduct. These conclusions describe the supplied selection only and do not establish how prevalent any view is among market analysts, consultancies or the press.

qs.q: Because every precedent’s authority must be independently verifiable, that burden falls on the lawyer, not the tool.
qs.a: When AI Becomes a Colleague: The Future of India's Legal Profession · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: In addition, the lawyer should send a written communication to the client that identifies the risks and limitations of these transcription and recording tools, including concerns about potentially waiving the attorney-client privilege and possible disclosure of confidential information to third parties (e.g., to the service provider transcribing or recording the call).
qs.a: Loss Prevention Takeaways — You, Me, and ChatGPT: How firms can educate clients about the dangers of uploading privileged or confidential information into GenAI platforms · Market & press · 2025

vlens.an:
This curated set of regulators, courts and professional bodies accepts the proposition’s core and materially develops it into enforceable governance. Across jurisdictions, the common position is that AI may assist legal or judicial work but cannot absorb professional responsibility: signatories, supervisors, court users and judges must exercise independent judgment, verify authorities and substantive propositions, protect confidentiality, and correct errors. Courts commonly justify this approach by the plausibility of fabricated or misrepresented material, the disproportionate checking burden imposed on opponents and courts, and the institutional harms to accurate adjudication and public confidence. Sanctions decisions generally focus on deficient inquiry, supervision and post-discovery candor, with mental state, scale, prior warnings, correction and cooperation affecting outcomes rather than AI use automatically triggering punishment.

Material internal variation concerns the supplementary controls needed beyond ordinary duties. Some authorities regard existing signature, competence and sanctions rules as sufficient and reject routine AI-use disclosure; others require certifications, declarations, tool identification or recordkeeping. Several adopt stricter task-specific boundaries for witness evidence, expert reports, autonomous court communications and judicial decision-making. Sanctions standards also vary with the governing source of authority: objective reasonable-inquiry rules may not require bad faith, whereas inherent-power sanctions ordinarily do. Guidance addressing self-represented litigants recognises a further tension between equal filing responsibility and limited practical capacity to verify legal output. A small amount of evidence redirects toward adjacent issues—most notably privilege for client-created AI documents—but does not challenge the principal proposition. These patterns describe the supplied sources only and should not be treated as showing how prevalent any position is among regulators, courts or professional bodies generally.

qs.q: In any case, whether Kiousenterlis used AI to conduct her research or not, citing non- existent cases, quotations, and specific propositions of law for which they do not stand and/or do not support, is unethical and sanctionable conduct.
qs.a: Cassata v. Michael Macrina Architect, P.C. — AI sanctions decision, Suffolk County · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: Subject to paragraph 23 below, Gen AI must not be used to draft or prepare the     content of an expert report (or any part of an expert report) without prior leave of     the Court.
qs.a: Supreme Court of NSW Practice Note SC Gen 23 — Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (issued 28 January 2025) · Regulators & courts · 2025

vlens.an: This anonymous frontline-practitioner thread supports the proposition’s core claim that human accountability and verification remain necessary when legal work is produced with AI. The strongest practitioner contribution accepts AI’s potential to save time on duplication and summarisation but insists that a knowledgeable human review the output and make it fit for purpose. The Federal Court of Australia guidance quoted in the thread also aligns with the cluster’s technology-neutral starting point: existing legal and professional responsibilities continue to govern, while non-use or transparency may be appropriate in particular circumstances rather than through a universal disclosure rule. There is material internal variation because the thread combines different anonymous posters and quoted institutional guidance rather than presenting a single unified practitioner view. Other comments defend willingness-to-pay pricing or predict major job losses and fee reductions; those claims neither undermine nor substantively develop the proposition about hallucination governance, inquiry failures and sanctions. The thread offers anecdotal evidence of allegedly poor AI-generated reports but does not address sanctions doctrine, organisational controls or measured model reliability. As a curated anonymous discussion, it should not be treated as representative of frontline practitioners generally.

qs.q: I can see how time can be saved on the actual grunt work of duplicating and summarising text, but a human who knows what they are doing needs to review the output and make it fit for purpose.
qs.a: Recently had a deeper look at the capability of an AI platform (RollOnFriday discussion-board thread) · Frontline practitioners · 2026

qs.q: This requires users of Generative AI to be guided by, and act in accordance with, their existing legal and professional responsibilities.[3] It follows that there will be circumstances where it is inappropriate to use Generative AI at all or where users ought to be transparent about its use.
qs.a: Recently had a deeper look at the capability of an AI platform (RollOnFriday discussion-board thread) · Frontline practitioners · 2026

vlens.an: The legal-tech vendor source supports the cluster’s principal proposition. Thomson Reuters treats AI as assistive rather than authoritative, places responsibility on the human lawyer, and requires independent verification against primary legal authorities before reliance. It also agrees that existing, technology-neutral duties—particularly filing certification and professional competence—already govern AI-assisted work. Its use of incidents involving lawyers, self-represented litigants and a judge reinforces the cluster’s account of concrete risks across the legal system without presenting those incidents as general model-error measurements. The main source-level variation is commercial and strategic rather than doctrinal: it asserts, without comparative measurements in the supplied evidence, that legal-specific platforms present lower hallucination risks than consumer tools and that verification workflows can confer competitive advantage. Those claims narrow the preferred implementation route but do not weaken its clear support for human accountability and broad verification. Because this facet contains one curated source, the assessment characterises that source only and does not imply that it represents legal-tech vendors generally.

qs.q: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11 and its state counterparts establish clear certification requirements for court filings, making attorneys personally responsible for verifying all submitted content, regardless of its technological origin.
qs.a: From 'trust but verify' to 'do not trust until verified': How the legal profession is redefining AI accountability · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

elens.an:
The curated 2023–2024 sources strongly support the cluster’s principal proposition. Courts, ethics bodies, professional task forces and commentators generally treat the generative-AI shock as creating new factual risks—especially fabricated authorities and confidently presented errors—without displacing established human duties of competence, candor, supervision and reasonable inquiry. Reported sanctions and referrals are tied principally to failures to check authorities, false or baseless submissions, inadequate supervision, or aggravating conduct after errors were identified; sanctions are not treated as an automatic consequence of using AI. Outcomes remain circumstance-specific, ranging from dismissal, costs, monetary penalties, suspension and disciplinary referral to declined sanctions accompanied by prospective warnings.

The main internal variation concerns supplementary governance rather than accountability itself. Technology-neutral sources argue that existing signature, procedural and professional-conduct rules are sufficient and that routine disclosure is redundant, difficult to define and potentially chilling as AI becomes embedded in ordinary software. Stricter approaches require disclosure, tool identification or human-review certification, and some restrict AI-assisted legal briefing or evidence preparation. Intermediate regimes trigger disclosure when AI acts like a co-author or when provenance is material. Several sources also develop the proposition beyond citation hallucinations by requiring tool-specific reliability evidence, organisational policies, confidentiality controls, judicial competence, transparent human reasoning and safeguards against fabricated evidence and deepfakes. More optimistic commentary predicts improving reliability or regards sanctions as sufficient deterrence, but still retains human supervision. Access-to-justice discussions expose a further tension: self-represented litigants remain formally responsible, although they may lack the legal knowledge and database access needed for meaningful verification. These differences substantiate the synthesis’s task-sensitive, bounded-adoption framework rather than opposing it. Because the corpus is curated, this alignment describes the supplied sources only and does not establish the prevalence of these views among courts, lawyers or regulators generally.

qs.q: The brief presents a false statement of law to this Court, and it appears that Attorney Lee made no inquiry, much less the reasonable inquiry required by Rule 11 and long-standing precedent, into the validity of the arguments she presented.
qs.a: Park v. Kim — Second Circuit opinion referring counsel to the Grievance Panel for a ChatGPT-fabricated citation · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: this case, the division declines to impose sanctions against the  appellant, but it puts lawyers and self-represented parties on notice  that future filings containing GAI-generated hallucinations may  may result in sanctions.
qs.a: Al-Hamim v. Star Hearthstone, LLC — First Colorado Appellate Ruling on GAI Hallucinations: Sanctions Declined for a Self-Represented Litigant, with Prospective Warning · Regulators & courts · 2024

elens.an:
The curated 2025 sources strongly support the cluster’s principal proposition that legal AI remains assistive, humans retain responsibility, and sanctions should address deficient inquiry or related conduct rather than AI use by itself. Across judicial decisions, ethics opinions and institutional policies, the recurring reasons are that plausible AI output may contain nonexistent authorities, false quotations or mischaracterisations of genuine cases; existing duties of competence, candor, supervision and reasonable inquiry already require independent verification; and responsibility follows the lawyer, signatory, supervisor or judge who relies on the work. The period’s sources also reinforce bounded adoption rather than prohibition, recognising possible efficiency and access benefits while requiring authoritative-source checking, confidentiality safeguards and retained human judgment.

Material variation concerns supplementary governance, not the accountability principle. Some authorities treat ordinary professional and procedural rules as sufficient and reject automatic disclosure, whereas others require certifications, tool identification, approved products, training, recordkeeping or prior permission. Restrictions are especially stringent for witness evidence, expert reports and judicial decision-making. Sanctions analysis also varies with governing doctrine and facts: objective inquiry failure may suffice under Rule 11, while inherent-power sanctions can require bad faith or its equivalent; prompt correction and candor may mitigate, while concealment, repeated failures, ignored warnings and ineffective supervision aggravate. Several sources materially extend the proposition to organisational implementation, client use and the limited verification capacity of self-represented litigants. Experimental work adds that retrieval grounding can reduce fabricated sources but citation verification alone does not establish overall work quality, and benefits vary by task. Two citation-only excerpts are too incomplete to reveal a governance position, but they do not supply contrary evidence.

qs.q: All legal representatives are responsible for the material they put before the court/tribunal and have a professional obligation to ensure it is accurate and appropriate.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence (AI) — Guidance for Judicial Office Holders (refreshed 31 October 2025) · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: Whether that conduct supports the imposition of various types of 14   sanctions requires a fact- and circumstance-specific analysis.
qs.a: Lacey v. State Farm General Ins. Co. — Special Master Order Sanctioning Ellis George and K&L Gates for AI-Generated Fake Citations · Regulators & courts · 2025

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources collectively accept the proposition’s central conduct-focused framework: AI does not displace the responsibility of lawyers, judges or filing parties; verification requires substantive human judgment rather than merely confirming that a citation exists; and sanctions generally respond to false material, deficient inquiry, supervision failures and post-discovery candor rather than to AI use itself. They materially develop that framework in several directions: California guidance sets boundaries for agentic systems and autonomous court-facing action; court decisions refine proportionality, signatory and supervisory liability, and mitigation or aggravation through correction and candor; benchmark research identifies potentially rising aggregate verification burdens and proposes automated checking and public legal-data access; and other sources extend the risk analysis to privilege, malpractice, insurance, confidentiality, legal education and possible erosion of legal reasoning. Material variation remains. Authorities disagree over mandatory disclosure, certification and task-specific prohibitions, while judicial chambers range from conditional use to prohibition. Access-to-justice sources accept filing accountability but question whether self-represented litigants can meaningfully satisfy it without structural support. Privilege sources shift attention to fact-specific confidentiality questions, and the legal-scholarship source redirects from accuracy to whether machine-written work can evidence authorial understanding. Incident reports and databases document court events but do not establish general model error rates; controlled benchmark findings are narrower and task-specific. These patterns describe this curated selection only and do not establish the prevalence of any view among courts, regulators, judges or practitioners.

qs.q: The duty to verify, the duty of candor, the duty of competence, and the duty of supervision cannot be delegated to a machine.
